title: Smart Tag vs. Tile: Samsung Tracker Comparison 2026
summary: Enjoy and learn from Life360's blog archive, focused on user life stories and experiences with our premier family safety app.
body_text: Summary What this article covers: A clear, head-to-head comparison of the Samsung Galaxy SmartTag and Tile by Life360, including phone compatibility, Bluetooth range, UWB precision finding, battery life, finding-network size, and price, so that you can pick the right tracking device for your phone and your life. Who it’s for Android users trying to decide between a smart tag and a Tile Samsung Galaxy owners weighing whether to stay inside the Samsung ecosystem Mixed iPhone-and-Android households that need one tracker everyone can use Anyone who has torn the house apart looking for keys, a wallet, or a bag People who want their stuff, their people, and their pets on a single map Key Takeaways The Samsung Galaxy SmartTag only works if you own a Samsung Galaxy device and a Samsung account. Tile works across both Android and iOS, so it fits almost any phone and any household. Tile relies on a worldwide network and a replaceable battery on the Tile Pro, plus a two-way find to ring your phone. The biggest difference is the bigger picture: Tile lives inside Life360, so your trackers share one map with your family and pets. You put your keys down for one second. Now they have vanished into the couch, the coat pocket, the junk drawer, or some fourth dimension that only exists when you are already late. A small tracking device on your keychain fixes that, and in 2026, two names come up repeatedly for Android users: the Samsung Galaxy SmartTag and Tile . They look almost identical. Both are little tags you clip onto the stuff you cannot afford to lose. Both ping your phone over a Bluetooth connection . Both lean on a network of other phones to help find things that wander out of range. So which one belongs on your keys ? The right smart tag depends almost entirely on the phone in your pocket. The longer version is a fair fight worth understanding before you spend the money, because these two trackers solve the same problem in very different ways. How Smart Tags Actually Work A smart tag is a coin-sized device that answers one question: Where did my stuff go? Underneath that simple job is a two-part system worth knowing before you compare brands. The first part is the Bluetooth connection between the tag and your phone. When the tag is nearby, your phone talks to it directly and can make it ring, or guide you the last few feet to the cushion it slipped under. This is the everyday magic, and it covers most where are my keys moments. The second part kicks in when your item is genuinely lost, far from your phone and out of Bluetooth range. That is where the finding network matters. Instead of relying on satellites, a smart tag taps into the network of other phones running the same app. When any of those phones passes near your lost tag, it quietly and anonymously updates the tag's location on your map. The bigger the network, the better your odds of seeing your bag pop up across town. Both the Samsung SmartTag and Tile use this same playbook. The differences come down to which phones can join the party, how far the Bluetooth reaches, and a few clever extras. Let's look at each tracker on its own first. Samsung Galaxy SmartTag: Built for the Galaxy Ecosystem If you are deep in the Galaxy world, the Samsung SmartTag has real advantages worth taking seriously. What the Samsung Smart Tag Does Well The Samsung Galaxy SmartTag2 reaches up to 120 meters (roughly 394 feet) over Bluetooth in open space with no walls in the way. That is a longer leash than most competitors. Battery life is another standout: The SmartTag2 runs on a swappable CR2032 coin cell and lasts up to about 500 days in normal use, stretching to roughly 700 days in power saving mode. When the battery finally dies, you pop the device open, drop in a fresh CR2032, and snap it shut in about ten seconds. Setup is quick if you have the right phone. You open the SmartThings app, hold the button on the tag, and it pairs. From there, you simply register the tag to your Samsung account, and you are tracking. The SmartTag also taps into SmartThings Find, Samsung's finding network, which uses other opted-in Galaxy devices to help locate your tag when it drifts out of Bluetooth range. UWB technology, short for Ultra-Wideband, gives you precise location down to close range on supported Galaxy phones, with an AR finding mode that puts directional arrows on your screen and walks you right to the item. The tag's programmable button can trigger custom routines and even control compatible IoT devices in your smart home. For someone living inside the Galaxy ecosystem, the SmartTag feels like a natural extension of the phone they already love. The Catch With Every Samsung SmartTag However, the Samsung Galaxy SmartTag only works with a Samsung Galaxy device. Not Android in general. Samsung specifically. You need a Galaxy phone or tablet, the SmartThings app, and a Samsung account login to register and use the tag at all. If you own a Pixel, a Motorola, a OnePlus, or any non-Samsung Android phone, the SmartTag is simply not an option. The UWB precision finding and AR features narrow things even further, since they only run on UWB-enabled Galaxy models. And if your household mixes an iPhone with an Android phone, the iPhone user is completely locked out. The SmartTag is a great tracker for a specific person. That person owns a recent Galaxy phone and plans to keep buying Galaxy phones. For everyone else, it simply won’t work. Your keys deserve a tracker that works with your phone. Full stop. Tile fits Android and iPhone alike — no Samsung account, no ecosystem lock-in, just your stuff showing up on the map where it belongs. See Life360 plans Tile by Life360: Built to Work With Any Phone Tile took the opposite approach. Instead of building the best tracker for one phone brand, Tile built a tracker that works with almost all phone brands. A Tile tracker pairs with both Android and iOS , so it does not care whether you carry a Galaxy, a Pixel, or an iPhone, or whether your family carries a mix of all three. You install the Life360 app , connect the tracker , and you are set. That cross-platform flexibility is the entire point, and it is the single biggest reason Tile keeps showing up on best-tracker lists for Android users who do not own a Samsung phone. The lineup covers whatever you are trying to keep track of. The Tile Pro is the long-range flagship, with a Bluetooth reach of around 500 feet and the only replaceable battery in the family, so you swap the cell instead of tossing the tag. The Tile is the everyday all-rounder for keys and bags. The Tile Slim slides into a wallet or passport sleeve. The Tile Sticker peels and sticks straight onto a remote, a laptop, or anything without a hole to loop through. Tile also has a feature Samsung does not match in the same way: two-way find. Press the button on your Tile, and it rings your phone, even when it's on silent. Lost the keys, you find them with the app. Lost the phone, you find it with the keys. And a triple-press on the Tile Pro sends an SOS alert to your emergency contacts via Life360, turning a key finder into a small safety tool. Smart Tag vs Tile: The Head-to-Head Here is how the two trackers stack up on the things that actually shape daily use. Feature Samsung Galaxy SmartTag2 Tile (by Life360) Works with Samsung Galaxy devices only Android and iOS Samsung account required Yes No Bluetooth range Up to ~394 ft (120 m) Up to ~500 ft (Tile Pro) UWB precision finding Yes, on supported Galaxy phones No Battery CR2032, up to ~500–700 days Replaceable on Tile Pro; ~3-yr sealed on others Finding network SmartThings Find (Samsung devices) Tile network across Android and iOS Two-way find (ring your phone) Limited Yes Typical price Around $29 $25 (Mate) to $35 (Pro) Keys. Kids. Pets. One map. Life360 puts your Tile trackers right alongside your family and pets — so "where is everything?" finally has one answer instead of four apps. See Life360 plans A few key takeaways from the table. Samsung wins raw range, UWB precision, and headline battery numbers. Tile wins compatibility, two-way find, and the replaceable battery on the Pro. Pricing lands close enough that it should not be your deciding factor. The finding-network comparison deserves a note because it is not as simple as a single number. Samsung's SmartThings Find draws on a large base of Galaxy devices, but only Galaxy devices. Tile's network spans both Android and iPhone users running the app. Which network finds your bag faster depends on what phones happen to be walking past it, and that depends a lot on where you live and travel. Which Tracking Device Is Right for You? Your phone makes this decision for you most of the time. If you own a recent Samsung Galaxy phone, plan to stay with Samsung, and want the absolute tightest close-range finding, get the SmartTag2. The UWB precision, long range, and deep SmartThings integration are helpful, and you will use them. You bought into the galaxy ecosystem, and the SmartTag is built to reward exactly that. If you own any other Android phone, get Tile . A Pixel, a Motorola, a OnePlus, a Nothing phone: none of them can use a Samsung smart tag, and Tile works with all of them out of the box. If your household is a mix of iPhones and Android devices, get Tile . This is the most common real-life situation. One parent on an iPhone, a teen on a Galaxy, a kid on a hand-me-down Pixel: Tile is the only tracker that puts all of them on the same map. Why the Best Tracker Lives in One Family App A tracker that lives in its own app, with its own login and notifications, becomes one more thing to juggle. Your keys are in one app. Your teen's location is in another. Your dog's whereabouts are in a third. Every where is it question sends you hunting through a different icon. Tile is part of Life360, so your trackers do not sit in a silo. They share one map with the people you love and the pets who treat your fence as a suggestion. Slip a Tile on your keys , your kid's backpack, and your luggage, and they show up right alongside your family members and your Life360 Pet GPS . One app, one map, everyone and everything in the same place. That shared map is the whole idea behind Life360. A smart tag answers Where are my keys? Life360 answers where is everyone, and is everything okay? which is the bigger question running in the back of your mind anyway. The Tile is the piece that brings your stuff into the picture, and it works with any phone you or anyone in your family carries. Which Tag Belongs on Your Keys The Samsung Galaxy SmartTag is a sharp little tracker, and if you live in the Galaxy world, it earns its place on your keys. But its biggest feature is also its biggest limit: it only works for Samsung owners, and only for the Samsung owners who stay that way. The moment your household includes another Android brand or an iPhone, you’re out of luck. Tile works with whatever phone you have, rings your phone back when the phone is the thing that went missing, and lives inside Life360, so your keys, your people, and your pets all land on one map. For most families, and for almost anyone who is not all-in on Samsung, that is the tracker that actually fits real life. Find the Tile that fits how you live, from the long-range Pro to the wallet-friendly Slim, and see how it all comes together on one map. Shop Tile trackers . Stop juggling apps. Start actually knowing. Life360 brings your stuff, your people, and your peace of mind into one place — whatever phone anyone in your family carries See Life360 plans

body_text: Liberty Latin America Announces 10-Year Strategic Engagement with Amdocs Liberty Latin America’s IT domain to be managed through Amdocs’ Agentic Operating System, aOS Agreement enhances IT operations, accelerates digital transformation, and drives significant technology cost savings Denver, Colorado and Jersey City, New Jersey - August 5, 2026: Liberty Latin America Ltd . (“Liberty Latin America” or the “Company”) (NASDAQ: LILA and LILAK, OTC Link: LILAB) today announced a 10-year strategic engagement with Amdocs (NASDAQ: DOX), a leading provider of software and services for communications and media companies, to manage its end-to-end IT ecosystem across its regional footprint. The engagement will transform Liberty Latin America’s traditional IT operations into an AI-driven operating model designed to accelerate time to market, increase product innovation, enhance customer and employee experience, and deliver significant cost savings. title: Paint the Shore with the Perfect Beach Photoshoot Poses
summary: Beach photoshoot poses that work with wind, glare and sand: shoreline walks, seated poses, silhouettes and golden-hour options.
body_text: Everything that makes a beach beautiful also makes it hard to shoot An open beach at two in the afternoon is one of the least forgiving places to photograph a person. The sun is directly overhead, the sand throws light back up into everyone's faces, there is no shade for a quarter of a mile, and the wind is doing something unhelpful to hair. None of which is an argument against beach sessions. It is an argument for planning one properly, because the same location an hour before sunset is about as good as photography gets. Low sun across the water, wet sand acting as a mirror, and a horizon that gives every frame somewhere to breathe. So the first decision is not which pose. It is what time, and after that the poses mostly take care of themselves. Timing, which decides everything else The hour or so before sunset is the window. Faces are lit softly from the side, nobody is squinting, and hair gets a rim of light that no amount of editing reproduces. Midday is the one to avoid. If you are stuck with it, get into the water rather than staying on dry sand, since the reflection fills the shadows under eyes, and keep everyone's backs to the sun. Our notes on the best and worst options for outdoor photo light cover the principle, and the sunset guides help with picking a stretch of coast. There are lists for where to photograph the sunset in San Diego and sunset spots in Miami . Solo poses on a beach Walking the shoreline is first and best. Walk parallel to the water, ankle-deep, and let the photographer shoot from the side and slightly behind. Look down at the water rather than at the camera for half the frames. Seated in the sand is second, and it works because low camera angles put the horizon behind your head instead of cutting across your neck. Legs folded to one side, one hand in the sand, weight leaning onto that arm. For wind, work with it rather than against it. Stand so the breeze comes from the side or slightly behind and lifts hair away from your face, since wind straight into your face pushes hair across your eyes and flattens clothing against you. Couple poses that suit the setting The shallow-water walk is the one to plan the session around. Hands linked, ankle-deep, talking to each other rather than performing. Silhouettes belong to the last fifteen minutes of light. Face each other at the water's edge with the sun directly behind, foreheads together or in a kiss, and let the photographer expose for the sky. The shapes have to be clean, which means space between your bodies and separated limbs, because a silhouette with no gaps reads as one dark blob. The back hug facing the water works in any light. It solves height differences on its own, and neither of you has to hold an expression. Family and kids on sand Sand is an advantage with small children, because it is the one location where a child sitting down and digging is a photograph rather than a lost frame. Get everyone low. Sitting or kneeling in the sand puts adult and child faces at similar heights, which is the biggest single improvement available in family beach frames. Walking as a group works if you keep it loose and let the kids run, and frames where nobody is looking at the camera are the point rather than the failure. Do the one organised group frame first, while patience lasts. What to wear so the wind works for you Fabric that moves is the whole point. A long dress or a loose shirt catches the breeze and gives the frame motion a fitted outfit cannot. Avoid anything that needs constant adjusting, because if you are holding a strap or a hem in place, that is what your hands will be doing in every photograph. Barefoot photographs better than shoes on sand and removes the question of footwear entirely. Light and mid tones hold up better against bright sand and water than dense black, which tends to flatten into a shape in strong backlight. Book a beach photoshoot Beach sessions live or die on timing, which is the argument for someone whose job is knowing when to be where. With Snappr, booking takes about 90 seconds and edited photos come back within 48 hours, with as little as 24 hours' notice. Book a beach photographer and get the hour that matters. Frequently asked questions What are the best poses for beach photos? Walking the shallows parallel to the water, seated low in the sand with legs folded to one side, and a backlit silhouette at the water's edge. For couples, the shallow-water walk and a back hug facing the water are the most reliable. What time of day is best for beach photos? The hour before sunset, or the hour after sunrise. Low side light stops people squinting and gives hair a rim of light. If you are stuck with midday, get into the shallows so the water fills the shadows under everyone's eyes. How do I stop squinting in beach photos? Keep the sun behind or to the side of you rather than in front. If you have to face it, look down, close your eyes and open them on a count of three so the frame lands before your face tenses. Shooting near the water helps too, since reflected light is softer than direct sun. What should I wear for a beach photoshoot? Something that moves in the wind, like a long dress or a loose shirt, and nothing that needs constant adjusting. Go barefoot rather than fighting shoes on sand. Light and mid tones read better against bright sand than dense black.

title: Best Shampoos for Wavy Hair: Dermatologist-Recommended Picks
summary: Confused about choosing a shampoo for wavy hair? Explore the best shampoos, must have ingredients & simple tips for healthy, defined waves.
body_text: Wavy Hair Choosing Shampoo for Wavy Hair Ingredients to Look For Top 5 Shampoos for Wavy Hair Mistakes to Avoid FAQs Wavy hair can look soft, bouncy, and well defined, but caring for it often feels like a puzzle. If your hair is neither completely straight nor tightly curly, choosing the best shampoo for wavy hair starts with understanding your hair's unique needs. Some shampoos, especially those with strong cleansing agents, may remove too much natural oil, leaving wavy hair dry, frizzy, or difficult to style. Using the right shampoo for wavy hair can help cleanse the scalp while maintaining moisture and supporting your natural wave pattern. Whether you need a gentle everyday cleanser or a sulfate free shampoo for wavy hair, choosing the right formula can make your styling routine easier. This guide explains how to care for wavy hair, which ingredients to look for, and which shampoos can help keep your waves healthy, soft, and defined. What Is Wavy Hair? Wavy hair sits between straight and curly hair on the hair type spectrum. It is commonly classified as Type 2 hair, falling between straight hair, or Type 1, and curly hair, or Type 3. Wavy hair usually forms a loose S shaped pattern that bends gently instead of creating tight curls or coils. Wavy hair can range from soft, barely visible waves to thicker and more defined patterns. It is often divided into Type 2A, Type 2B, and Type 2C, depending on the strength and shape of the waves. What Makes Wavy Hair Different? Wavy hair has a curved structure that affects how it looks, feels, and responds to hair care products. Its pattern is shaped by several genetic, biological, and structural factors. These characteristics also influence how moisture and natural oils move through the hair. The main factors that make wavy hair different include: Hair Structure: Wavy hair has a loose S-shaped pattern that gives it natural movement and volume without forming tight curls. Oil Distribution: Natural oils do not spread evenly through the bends of wavy hair, which can leave the roots oilier and the mid lengths and ends drier. Moisture Retention: The bends in wavy hair can make it more prone to dryness and frizz because natural oils do not spread evenly along the hair shaft. Why Does Wavy Hair Need a Different Shampoo? Wavy hair has different cleansing needs than straight hair. Its natural bends make it harder for scalp oils to spread evenly from the roots to the ends. As a result, the scalp may feel oily while the lengths and ends become dry. A shampoo made for wavy hair should help address these concerns by: Maintaining Moisture: It cleanses the scalp without removing too much of the hair's natural moisture. Reducing Frizz: It helps keep the hair smoother and easier to manage. Supporting Wave Definition: It helps maintain your natural wave pattern without making the hair feel stiff or heavy. Providing Balanced Cleansing: It removes excess oil, dirt, and product buildup while keeping the hair hydrated. Some shampoos contain strong cleansing agents that may remove too much natural oil, leaving wavy hair feeling dry and rough. Others contain heavier conditioning ingredients that may weigh down fine waves and reduce their natural volume. How to Choose the Best Shampoo for Wavy Hair Not every shampoo is suitable for wavy hair. The right formula should cleanse the scalp effectively while helping maintain moisture and support your natural wave pattern. Here are some of the factors to consider when choosing the shampoo for wavy hair: Avoid Heavy Residue: Some shampoos leave a coating on the hair that can make waves look flat. Choose formulas that cleanse well without leaving your hair feeling heavy. Consider Sulfate-free Formulas: Consider a sulfate free shampoo for wavy hair if your hair is dry, colour treated, or prone to frizz, as these formulas are generally gentler than sulfate based cleansers. Match Your Scalp Type: Many people with wavy hair have oilier roots and drier ends. Choose a shampoo that suits your scalp type without drying the lengths. Look for Hydrating Ingredients: Ingredients such as glycerin, aloe vera, shea butter, and plant oils can help reduce frizz and improve softness. Choose Lightweight Formulas: Heavy products can weigh down waves and reduce their natural bounce. Lightweight moisturizing shampoos are often a better choice for fine or loose waves. What Ingredients Should You Look for in a Shampoo for Wavy Hair? The ingredients in your shampoo play an important role in keeping wavy hair healthy and manageable. Look for ingredients that help cleanse gently, maintain moisture, and reduce frizz without weighing your waves down. Some of the most beneficial ingredients include: Aloe vera: Helps hydrate the hair and soothe the scalp while keeping the hair soft and manageable. Glycerin : A humectant that attracts moisture to the hair, helping reduce dryness and improve softness. Argan Oil : A lightweight oil that helps nourish the hair, reduce frizz, and add natural shine. Jojoba Oil: Helps moisturise the hair and scalp without leaving a heavy or greasy feel. Coconut Oil: Helps reduce protein loss from the hair, making it beneficial for dry or damaged wavy hair. Shea Butter: Rich in fatty acids that help moisturise dry hair, reduce frizz, and improve softness, especially in thicker waves. Hydrolyzed Proteins : Ingredients such as hydrolyzed rice, wheat, or soy protein can temporarily strengthen damaged hair and improve smoothness. 5 Best Shampoos for Wavy Hair With so many shampoos available, choosing the right one can be confusing. The best option depends on your hair texture, scalp condition, and individual hair concerns. To make your search easier, we have curated a list of dermatologist curated shampoos for wavy hair along with their key ingredients and benefits: Product Key Ingredients Benefits Beauty Garage Pure African Shea Butter Retention Treatment Wavy Curl Shampoo Shea Butter, Citric Acid Gently cleanses, deeply moisturises, reduces frizz, and enhances natural wave definition. Curl Up Curl Moisturising Shampoo Argan Oil, Jojoba Oil Hydrates the hair, controls frizz, and helps maintain soft, well-defined waves. Deyga Rice Water Shampoo Rice Water, Glycerin Cleanses gently, nourishes the hair, and improves softness and shine. The Curl Co Cleanse & Hydrate Curl Shampoo Shea Butter, Quinoa Protein Removes buildup while providing lasting hydration and improving manageability. Manetain Moisturising Shampoo Glycerin, Seaweed Extract Balances moisture, reduces frizz, and supports smoother, healthier looking waves. 1. Beauty Garage Pure African Shea Butter Retention Treatment Wavy Curl Shampoo If your wavy hair feels dry, frizzy, or difficult to manage, this shampoo offers a nourishing cleanse without stripping away natural moisture. Formulated with pure African shea butter, proteins, and amino acids, it is designed to improve hair health while enhancing the natural texture of waves and curls. Here are some of its key benefits: Gently Cleanses Without Drying: Removes dirt and buildup while helping preserve the hair's natural oils. Helps Reduce Frizz: Shea butter provides lasting moisture to improve smoothness and manageability. Helps Strengthens the Hair Fibres: Proteins and amino acids help support stronger, healthier looking hair. 2. Curl Up Curl Moisturising Shampoo Designed for wavy and curly hair, this shampoo focuses on maintaining the right balance between cleansing and hydration. Its lightweight formula helps keep the hair fresh while supporting soft, bouncy waves, making it suitable for regular wash days. Let's look at its key benefits: Cleanses Gently: Removes excess oil and impurities without making the hair feel dry. Maintains Moisture Balance: Argan oil and plant based ingredients help keep the hair soft and manageable. Improves Bounce: Helps waves look more defined and full of life with regular use. 3. Deyga Rice Water Shampoo If you prefer naturally inspired hair care, this rice water shampoo offers gentle cleansing while nourishing both the scalp and hair. The formula contains fermented rice water along with botanical extracts to support healthier looking hair. Here are some of its key benefits: Supports Stronger Hair: Rice water contains amino acids that may help improve the feel and appearance of the hair. Promotes a Healthy Scalp: Botanical ingredients help keep the scalp clean and comfortable. Adds Natural Shine: Regular use helps improve softness and the overall appearance of dull hair. 4. The Curl Co Cleanse & Hydrate Curl Shampoo This shampoo is formulated to remove everyday buildup while keeping wavy and curly hair hydrated. Enriched with quinoa, shea butter, sunflower, and argan, it helps cleanse the hair without compromising moisture. Here are some of the reasons it stands out: Removes Dirt and Product Buildup: Cleanses the scalp effectively while maintaining hydration. Helps Improve Hair Strength: Quinoa helps support stronger hair and reduce breakage. Protects and Nourishes Hair: Shea butter and nourishing plant ingredients help keep hair soft and manageable. 5. Manetain Moisturising Shampoo This shampoo is suitable for dry or frizz prone wavy hair that needs both hydration and protein support. It combines moisturising ingredients with proteins to improve manageability while helping maintain healthy looking waves. Here are some of its key benefits: Balances Protein and Moisture: Helps maintain the right balance for soft, healthy looking hair. Improves Manageability: Reduces frizz and makes the hair easier to detangle and style. Supports Healthy Looking Waves: It helps maintain soft, defined, and manageable waves. Hair Care Tips for Wavy Hair Choosing the best shampoo for wavy hair is only one part of a healthy hair care routine. The way you wash, dry, and style your hair also affects how your waves look and feel. Here are some simple hair care tips for wavy hair that can help reduce frizz , improve manageability, and maintain your natural wave pattern: Detangle While Conditioning: Use a wide toothed comb to detangle your hair while the conditioner is still on. Avoid brushing dry hair. Use a Microfiber Towel: Dry your hair with a microfiber towel or a soft cotton T shirt to reduce friction and frizz. Apply Styling Products to Damp: This helps distribute the product evenly and support better wave definition. Limit Heat Styling: Reduce the use of heat styling tools and always apply a heat protectant before styling. Trim Your Hair Regularly: Regular trims help minimize split ends and keep your waves looking healthy. How to Wash Wavy Hair Correctly The way you wash your hair can affect how soft, healthy, and defined your waves look. Using the right technique helps cleanse the scalp while protecting the lengths from unnecessary dryness. Here are some simple steps to help you wash your wavy hair effectively: Wet Your Hair Thoroughly: Use lukewarm water to completely soak your hair before applying shampoo. Focus on the Scalp: Apply shampoo to your scalp and gently massage it with your fingertips. Avoid using your nails, as they may irritate the scalp. Let the Lather Cleanse the Lengths: Avoid scrubbing the mid lengths and ends. As you rinse, the lather is usually enough to cleanse them. Rinse Thoroughly: Wash away all the shampoo to help prevent product buildup. Condition the Lengths: Apply conditioner from the mid lengths to the ends. Leave it on for two to three minutes before rinsing thoroughly. Dry Gently: Pat your hair dry with a microfiber towel or a soft cotton T shirt instead of rubbing it. Let your hair air dry whenever possible or use a diffuser on a low heat setting if needed. Common Mistakes People Make Even after choosing the best shampoo for wavy hair, your daily hair care habits can influence the health of your waves. Identifying and avoiding common mistakes can help reduce frizz and keep your hair easier to manage. Here are common mistakes to avoid when using shampoo on wavy hair: Washing Too Frequently: Over washing can make wavy hair dry and frizzy. Wash your hair based on your scalp type. Using Very Hot Water: Hot water can increase dryness and frizz. Use lukewarm water instead. Ignoring Scalp Care: Cleanse your scalp thoroughly to help prevent product buildup and excess oil. Using Too Much Product: Excess conditioner or styling products can weigh down your waves. Final Thoughts Choosing the best shampoo for wavy hair starts with understanding your hair's unique needs. The right formula should match your hair texture, scalp type, and individual concerns while providing gentle cleansing and balanced hydration. Since no single shampoo works for everyone, you may need to try different formulations before finding one that suits your hair best. Whether you are looking for a moisturizing shampoo for wavy hair or a sulfate free shampoo for wavy hair, pairing the right product with a consistent hair care routine can help reduce frizz, improve manageability, and support healthy looking waves. If you continue to experience persistent scalp concerns or excessive hair loss, consult a dermatologist for personalized advice.

(NASDAQ: HOUR) (“Hour Loop” or the “Company”), a leading online retailer, announces its financial and operational results for the quarter ended June 30, 2026 Financial
body_text: Hour Loop Reports Second Quarter of 2026 Results August 11, 2026 at 4:05 PM EDT PDF Version Continued Profitability Despite a Challenging Economic Environment Redmond, WA, Aug. 11, 2026 (GLOBE NEWSWIRE) -- Hour Loop, Inc. (NASDAQ: HOUR) (“Hour Loop” or the “Company”), a leading online retailer, announces its financial and operational results for the quarter ended June 30, 2026 Financial Highlights for Second Quarter of 2026: Net revenues increased 25% to $33.9 million, compared to $27.1 million in the year-ago period; Net income decreased to $1.1 million, compared to $1.2 million in the year-ago period; and Cash used in operating activities was $3.6 million, compared to cash used in operating activities of $0.9 million in the year-ago period. Management Commentary “This was a remarkable quarter for Hour Loop. Revenue grew 25% year over year, reflecting strong business momentum and giving us greater confidence in the opportunities ahead,” said Sam Lai, Chief Executive Officer and Interim Chief Financial Officer. “We delivered this growth while navigating margin pressure and continuing to improve how we operate. We are excited about what we have accomplished—and even more excited about what comes next.” “Our vision is to automate every part of the business. Humans are optional. We believe AI will fundamentally reshape how companies operate, and Hour Loop intends to lead in this new era. Our proprietary AI system already powers more than one hundred AI agents across the organization, and we are redesigning our operations around autonomous execution, faster decisions and greater scale. We believe 2026 will be remembered as the beginning of Hour Loop’s AI-first era.” “We are deeply grateful to our employees for their ambition and execution, and to our shareholders for their continued confidence. We believe the next several years can be transformative for Hour Loop, and we have never been more optimistic about the opportunity ahead.” Second Quarter of 2026 Financial Results Net revenues in the Second Quarter of 2026 were $33.9 million, compared to $27.1 million in the same period last year. The increase was primarily driven by expanded inventory availability, which supported improved product availability and sales execution. Gross profit as a percentage of net revenues decreased to 52.9%, compared to 57.2% in the same period last year. The decrease was primarily reflecting a shift in sales strategy. In the same period last year, the Company intentionally maintained a higher gross margin in response to tariff concerns by preserving lower-cost inventory and gradually adjusting retail prices to help customers adapt to higher price levels. Operating expenses as a percentage of net revenues in the Second Quarter of 2026 decreased to 49.2%, compared to 51.2% in the same period last year. The decrease was mainly attributable to greater operating leverage and continued efficiency improvements. Net income in the Second Quarter of 2026 was $1.1 million, or $0.03 per diluted share, compared to net income of $1.2 million, or $0.04 per diluted share, in the same period last year. The decrease was driven by increased costs and decreased expenses because of the reasons mentioned above. As of June 30, 2026, the Company had $1.0 million in cash and cash equivalents, compared to $3.8 million as of December 31, 2025. This decrease was driven by payments to related parties and additional investment in inventory. Full Year 2026 Financial Outlook Hour Loop reaffirms its guidance for the full year, anticipating 2026 net revenue to be in the range of $143.0 million to $163.0 million, representing flat to 15% year-over-year growth. The Company continues to expect 2026 net income to be in the range of $0.75 million to $1.5 million. About Hour Loop, Inc. Hour Loop is an online retailer engaged in e-commerce retailing in the U.S. market. It has operated as a third-party seller on www.amazon.com and has sold merchandise on its website at www.hourloop.com since 2013. Hour Loop further expanded its operations to other marketplaces such as Walmart, eBay, and SHEIN. To date, Hour Loop has generated practically all its revenue as a third-party seller on www.amazon.com and only a negligible amount of revenue from its own website and other marketplaces. Hour Loop manages more than 100,000 stock-keeping units (“SKUs”). Product categories include home/garden décor, toys, kitchenware, apparel, and electronics. Hour Loop’s primary strategy is to bring most of its vendors’ product selections to the customers. It has advanced software that assists Hour Loop in identifying product gaps so it can keep such products in stock year-round, including the entirety of the last quarter (holiday season) of the calendar year. In upcoming years, Hour Loop plans to expand its business rapidly by increasing the number of business managers, vendors, and SKUs. title: Introducing Managed Sandboxes and Filesystems for Mastra Platform
summary: You can now give every environment a persistent filesystem and secure sandboxes, provisioned and billed through the Mastra platform.
body_text: Some of the most capable agents being built today share a common trait: they have a computer to work with. That computer gives them a place to write files, run code, and leave behind work that outlasts a single conversation. While Mastra already supports connecting to any number of hosted sandbox providers, it's always meant a good deal of setup work to get up and running. Now, with sandboxes and filesystems on the Mastra platform, every environment in your project can get a bucket for persistent file storage and a sandbox for running commands, provisioned for you. Your browser does not support the video tag. Using the new @mastra/platform-workspace SDK, you can pull in both the PlatformFilesystem and PlatformSandbox primitives to put your filesystem and sandbox directly on the platform. The PlatformFilesystem acts as your agent's persistent filesystem: files your agent writes there (generated reports, working documents, code it's iterating on, etc.) survive across conversations, deploys, and restarts, so your agent can build a durable body of work instead of starting from scratch on every run. And the PlatformSandbox is where your agent safely executes the code it writes: commands run in an isolated environment away from your production server, and the platform keeps the sandbox base image warmed so the first call starts quickly. The platform handles everything around the providers. Filesystems and sandboxes are provisioned per environment, so production and staging each get their own bucket and sandbox, and your staging agent's files stay out of production's. Credentials are injected at deploy time as environment variables, which means the provider doesn’t require options on the platform, you construct them, deploy, and they connect. Billing is straightforward as well: they share your project's CPU time and data egress, with no separate infrastructure bill to manage. You can manage them all from the Workspaces tab in your project, which shows each environment's bucket contents with upload, download, and delete actions, along with recent sandbox sessions and their command, exit code, and duration. The same providers also work locally so you can put your environment's variables in a .env file and PlatformFilesystem and PlatformSandbox connect to the same bucket and sandbox pool you run in the cloud. Sandboxes are deployed in the same service provider as your Studio and Server, so all resources are automatically colocated for better performance and cost. Requirements Managed filesystems and sandboxes are enabled by default on new platform projects. For existing projects, open the Workspaces tab and select Enable workspaces , which provisions a bucket for every environment on the project. Your code needs the @mastra/platform-workspace package, which works with your existing Workspace configuration from @mastra/core . Get started in the CLI Install the provider package: Terminal npm install @mastra/platform-workspace Compose the providers into a workspace: src/mastra/workspaces/workspace.ts import { Workspace, LocalFilesystem, LocalSandbox } from " @mastra/core/workspace " ; import { PlatformFilesystem, PlatformSandbox } from " @mastra/platform-workspace " ; // platform providers when the injected credentials are present, // local equivalents otherwise const onPlatform = process.env.MASTRA_PLATFORM_ACCESS_TOKEN; export const workspace = new Workspace ({ filesystem: onPlatform ? new PlatformFilesystem () : new LocalFilesystem ({ basePath: " ./workspace " }), sandbox: onPlatform ? new PlatformSandbox () : new LocalSandbox ({ workingDirectory: " ./workspace " }), }); Register the workspace on your main Mastra instance: import { Mastra } from " @ mastra /core " ; import { workspace } from " ./workspaces/workspace " ; export const mastra = new Mastra ({ workspace }); Deploy your project — the workspace ships with it: Terminal mastra deploy Your agent now has file and command tools backed by managed infrastructure. Managed filesystems and sandboxes are in alpha, so expect the surface to evolve as we learn from real workloads (and tell us what your agents need next!). For more information and full configuration options, read our platform docs on workspaces and environments , and the PlatformFilesystem and PlatformSandbox references.

body_text: The North Carolina recruiting firm moved candidate sourcing off hand-built spreadsheets and onto filtered searches with automated outreach, cutting manual effort in half. VANCOUVER, Wash.--(BUSINESS WIRE)--Aug. 18, 2026-- ZoomInfo (NASDAQ: GTM), the all-in-one AI GTM platform, has reported that National Recruiting Network, a recruiting firm placing engineering, maintenance, and leadership talent in plastics and packaging manufacturing, has raised its candidate connection rates by 25% and cut its manual sourcing work by 50%, according to the company. It did so with a small team, in a labor market where every qualified candidate had options. National Recruiting Network was under two years old and growing fast. Its sourcing process was manual. Candidate information came out of various sources and went into Excel spreadsheets, work the firm describes as incredibly tedious and time consuming. For a large agency with a research department, that is a line item. For a firm this size, it was the workweek. Worse, the tedium was hiding a targeting problem. Plastics and packaging manufacturing roles require very specific expertise and education, and a spreadsheet assembled from whatever was findable cannot tell you who has that background. So the firm was contacting people who looked plausible rather than people who qualified. Its own stated baseline: reach out to 100 candidates, and one reply was a good day. Ninety-nine touches went nowhere. The firm changed three things with ZoomInfo, and each attacks a different part of that failure. First, precision. Detailed searches isolate candidates matching a specific expertise and education requirement, so in a niche like plastics processing the list is 40 qualified people instead of 500 plausible ones. Second, reach. Accurate contact data means the message lands in a live inbox rather than bouncing, and a bounce is a candidate the recruiter never knows was interested. Third, volume without headcount. The firm builds a separate automated outreach sequence per type of role, then sends it to the candidates those searches surface. Reporting shows which messaging works for which audience, so the pitch for a maintenance lead is tuned separately from the pitch for a process engineer. The results followed the mechanism. Candidate connection rates rose 25% against that one-reply-per-100 baseline, and manual effort fell by half, according to the company. The recovered hours went into relationship-building with candidates and clients instead of data entry. The firm reported its best month on record and a lower time to hire, which gave it room to take on more clients, and it credits ZoomInfo for the revenue that followed. The bet from here is capacity, not headcount. Each recruiter carries more searches, so the same small team serves more clients. In a niche where the qualified pool is narrow and the competition for it is not, finding the right 40 people beats reaching the wrong 500. Powered by the industry's most comprehensive B2B data, including more than 100 million companies, 500 million contacts, and billions of signals, ZoomInfo delivers the intelligence, automation, and integrations that modern revenue teams need to identify, engage, and convert their best buyers. title: Alliant Energy files rezoning application for proposed Morgan Valley Energy Center in Linn County
summary: Alliant Energy has submitted a rezoning application to Linn County for the proposed Morgan Valley Energy Center, a natural gas-fired electric generating facility planned near the intersection of U.S. 30 and Benton-Linn Road west of Cedar Rapids.
body_text: Alliant Energy files rezoning application for proposed Morgan Valley Energy Center in Linn County CEDAR RAPIDS, Iowa (July 16, 2026) — Alliant Energy has submitted a rezoning application to Linn County for the proposed Morgan Valley Energy Center , a natural gas-fired electric generating facility planned near the intersection of U.S. 30 and Benton-Linn Road west of Cedar Rapids. The application requests rezoning of approximately 160 acres from Agricultural (AG) to Exclusive Use-2 (EU-2), as required under Linn County's development code for gas-fired electric generating facilities. The proposed Morgan Valley Energy Center would consist of three natural gas combustion turbines with a combined generating capacity of approximately 720 megawatts. The project is designed to help meet growing energy needs, support electric reliability and meet regional capacity requirements. While proposed on 160 acres of land, the actual facility would only take up about 55 acres, with a portion of the land expected to be restored to agricultural use upon operation. "The submission of our zoning application reflects the next step in what is a thorough review process from multiple regulating entities," said May Farlinger, President of Alliant Energy's Iowa energy company. "Our application includes detailed information about the proposed project, including site planning, infrastructure needs and economic impacts. We remain committed to engaging with the community and participating fully in the county's review process." As part of the application, Alliant Energy submitted an independent economic impact analysis estimating the project could create approximately 200 jobs in Linn County and generate nearly $90 million in local economic output during construction. The company also anticipates significant opportunities for local contractors and suppliers and is committed to using qualified union labor whenever possible during construction. The analysis also suggests that more than $24 million in local tax revenue could be generated over the life of the facility. The rezoning application outlines opportunities for local contracting, procurement and workforce participation associated with the project. The rezoning application is separate from the project's air permitting application, which the company expects to submit to Linn County Public Health within the next week. The complete application will include air modeling results and detailed technical analyses, and will be available on the Iowa DNR’s EASY Air System . As required by law, it will be reviewed through a public process that is separate from the rezoning review process. Alliant Energy currently anticipates technical review of the air permit application to be completed in early 2027, followed by opportunities for public comment. Farlinger added, “Guided by our values and commitment to environmental stewardship, we approach every project with a focus on safety, compliance and accountability. Alliant Energy has decades of experience constructing and operating generating facilities while meeting stringent environmental standards and regulatory requirements, and we look forward to demonstrating this fact through the review process.” Over the coming months, Linn County will review the rezoning application through its established process, which includes multiple opportunities for public input before the Planning and Zoning Commission and Board of Supervisors. Community feedback will be considered alongside technical, planning and regulatory requirements throughout the review. To learn more about the proposed Morgan Valley Energy Center, visit Alliant Energy's website . About Alliant Energy Alliant Energy Corporation (NASDAQ: LNT) provides regulated energy service to more than 1 million electric and 435,000 natural gas customers across Iowa and Wisconsin. Alliant Energy's mission is to deliver energy solutions and exceptional service customers and communities count on – safely, efficiently and responsibly. Interstate Power and Light Company (IPL) and Wisconsin Power and Light Company (WPL) are Alliant Energy's two wholly-owned subsidiaries. For more information, visit alliantenergy.com and follow Alliant Energy on LinkedIn , Facebook , Instagram and X . title: The new CX AI operating model
summary: Learn how agentic AI is reshaping customer experience with orchestration, memory, governance, and autonomous resolution.
body_text: The new CX AI operating model by Andy Traba August 11, 2026 Share A few years ago, AI in customer experience meant assistance, with copilots suggesting responses, bots answering questions, and context that evaporated the moment a session ended. That era is over, and I don't say that as a prediction. Last week, Neeraj Verma, our VP of Product Management, and I spent an hour with thousands of CX, technology, and operations leaders unpacking what's replaced that time. The shift shows up across every dimension of technology. AI that could only assist has become agentic AI that resolves issues end to end. Context that resets after every session has become Experience Memory that compounds. Autonomy with limited oversight, the era of hallucinations and off-the-rails bots, has become governed, auditable action. And the fallback human role has become human and AI collaboration by design. When we polled our audience, 19% said they're already live with proactive AI outreach across multiple channels. The majority have it on the roadmap. This post and the webinar that inspired it address that gap between where most organizations are and where the technology has already gone. Watch the webinar Why point AI existed, and why it's ending Neeraj gave the clearest technical explanation for why the first wave of CX AI looked the way it did. "Why did you have point AI solutions? Because a year ago, two years ago, large language models had very small context windows," he explained. Discrete tasks were all the technology could reliably hold: a copilot here, knowledge retrieval there. As context windows expanded and reasoning improved, models became capable of orchestrating entire automation flows. But bigger context windows alone don't create value. "You've got a huge amount of context. What do you dump into it? What do you store?" Neeraj asked. The right context, at the right moment, drawn from the right memory is the difference between an AI agent that converses and an AI agent that resolves. The business results confirm the architecture argument. A 2026 Metrigy study found that organizations running enterprise-wide connected AI strategies see roughly double the improvement of point-AI organizations across every metric that matters, including employee satisfaction, customer ratings, efficiency, revenue, and cost. The value gap between point AI and orchestrated AI isn't theoretical anymore. It's showing up in the data. What orchestration looks like when it matters We built our demo around the scenario every CX leader dreads. A storm grounds flights nationwide and contact volume spikes 300%. Most operations break there. In the demo, the platform scaled instead. AI agents expanded capacity instantly to handle rebookings while human agents shifted to the complex, high-emotion moments, like a traveler racing to reach a sick family member. Context transferred between AI and human with no repetition. Supervisors managed one blended workforce from a single workspace. Behind the scenes, analytics detected the surge pattern and recommended a dedicated AI rebooking agent with preapproved policies, simulation-tested and live in minutes. Two days later, when the weather shifted again, impacted travelers were notified proactively before they ever picked up the phone. That's the difference between automating tasks and orchestrating outcomes. Here's what makes it possible. One engagement across every agent and channel Customer journeys now involve more participants than ever: consumers, their personal AI assistants, enterprise AI agents, and human employees, often within a single interaction. The Agentic Engagement Plane is the mediation layer that holds all of it together as one continuous engagement from intent to resolution, not a trail of fragmented contacts stitched together after the fact. "You need a unification for how those platforms communicate with your customers," as Neeraj put it. The same context, memory, and guardrails apply no matter which AI is talking. Measure resolution, not deflection The next generation of AI agents, powered by Cognigy technology now native to our platform, executes tools and takes action in enterprise systems. And they're becoming truly multimodal in the CX sense. An agent that talks with you on a call while texting a two-factor code, sharing a map, or accepting a photo and digital signature after a car accident. In our demo, the AI checked fare rules, found the flight, preserved preferences, and completed the transaction. The unit of value moves from contacts deflected to work completed. And that should change how you measure everything. Memory that makes every interaction smarter Experience Memory gives every AI agent, application, and human the same living picture of the customer, such as preferences, history, past events, and open commitments, available instantly at the start of every engagement. It also solves a problem most leaders haven't confronted yet: context poisoning. More context isn't better; the right context is. Reliable, continuously updated memory is what lets each engagement begin smarter than the one before. Governance is the gas pedal A point made in the webinar that I’d like to reiterate. Autonomy expands as fast as oversight, so think of governance as the gas pedal, not the brake. Guardian AI moves oversight from after-the-fact dashboards to runtime, monitoring conversations in real time and steering an agent back on track before a problem becomes an incident. It's no accident that some of our fastest-moving AI customers come from regulated industries. They already had the policies, and now they have a system that enforces them. Observability was the buzzword of the last few years. Governed action at runtime is what replaces it. Analytics that act Agentic Analytics flips analytics from a system of insight to a system of action. Fleets of AI agents analyze every piece of platform data and then act, updating agent instructions and even building new AI agents directly from engagement data when a new call type emerges. Neeraj's line on this deserves to be framed. "You cannot have compounding value without putting pennies in the same piggy bank." That's why the platform matters. Compounding requires everything in one place. One workforce, human and AI The workforce now includes both people and AI agents, and everything about workforce management changes as a result. Quality for an AI agent isn't measured like quality for a human, and staffing models look different when capacity can expand instantly. As AI absorbs routine execution, human work concentrates in complexity, ambiguity, empathy, judgment, and trust. My advice is to update your hiring profiles, coaching models, and quality frameworks before the rollout, not after. Where to start The innovations that matter are the ones that resolve, remember, and are governed. They fit together as one operating model orchestrated across the full customer experience, open to third-party systems. Foundations come first, data and integrations, because garbage in is still garbage out. Measure resolution, not deflection. And scale autonomy exactly as fast as your oversight can follow. Neeraj's closing advice is the right note of caution, "Data is probably the most important, most overlooked item when implementing an AI solution. Creating point solutions is not hard. What is hard is operating them at scale." Mine is the right note of ambition. Don't automate a password reset. Think big. The real dividing line for CX leaders right now is whether AI in your organization acts as one connected system. The future of CX AI belongs to the organization that can orchestrate intelligence across every interaction and turn that intelligence into continuously compounding value. Watch the full Orchestrating Intelligence webinar , and if you want to pressure-test your own roadmap against this operating model, my team would love to talk. Frequently Asked Questions Point AI refers to standalone tools that handle discrete tasks in isolation, such as a single copilot or a knowledge retrieval bot, without shared context or coordination across systems. Orchestrated AI connects agents, memory, governance, and analytics into one operating model that resolves issues end to end rather than just assisting with them. Organizations running enterprise-wide connected AI strategies see roughly double the improvement of point-AI organizations across metrics including employee satisfaction, customer ratings, efficiency, revenue, and cost, according to a 2026 Metrigy study. The gap between the two approaches shows up directly in business results rather than remaining a theoretical distinction. Early CX AI relied on point solutions because large language models had small context windows that could only reliably hold discrete tasks, limiting each tool to a narrow function like a single copilot or isolated knowledge lookup. As context windows expanded and reasoning improved, models gained the capacity to orchestrate entire automation flows rather than handling one task at a time. Expanding context alone does not create value; the technology also needs the right information stored and retrieved at the right moment. That combination of larger context and well-managed memory is what separates an AI agent that simply converses from one that resolves a customer's issue. Experience Memory is a shared, continuously updated record that gives every AI agent, application, and human employee the same real-time picture of a customer, including preferences, history, past events, and open commitments. It ensures each new interaction begins with full context already available rather than resetting after every session. Experience Memory also addresses context poisoning, the problem of feeding an AI system more information without ensuring it is the right information. Reliable memory, rather than simply more data, is what allows each customer engagement to be smarter than the one before it. Governance is described as a gas pedal because autonomy can expand only as fast as oversight allows, making strong governance the mechanism that enables faster AI deployment rather than a constraint that slows it down. Guardian AI illustrates this by monitoring conversations in real time and steering an agent back on track before a problem becomes an incident, shifting oversight from after-the-fact review to runtime intervention. Regulated industries have moved quickly with AI adoption partly because they already had established policies and now have systems that enforce those policies automatically. Governed action at runtime has replaced observability as the more advanced standard for managing AI behavior. Companies should measure work completed rather than contacts deflected, since AI agents built on the next generation of technology now execute tools and take real action inside enterprise systems rather than just answering questions. This includes checking fare rules, locating a flight, preserving customer preferences, and completing a transaction within a single interaction. These agents are also becoming multimodal, capable of talking on a call while simultaneously texting a verification code, sharing a map, or accepting a photo and digital signature. Shifting the measurement standard to resolution reflects the shift in what the AI itself is actually doing. AI changes workforce management by creating a blended workforce of people and AI agents managed together, which requires new approaches to quality measurement and staffing since AI agent quality cannot be evaluated using the same standards applied to human agents. As AI takes over routine, high-volume execution, human work concentrates on complexity, ambiguity, empathy, judgment, and trust, since capacity can now expand instantly through AI agents during demand spikes. Supervisors oversee this blended workforce from a single unified workspace rather than managing human and AI channels separately. Organizations are advised to update hiring profiles, coaching models, and quality frameworks before rolling out AI rather than adjusting them afterward. About the Author Andy Traba Andy Traba is Vice President of Product Marketing at NiCE, where he establishes the narrative for AI platform innovation and its real customer and business impact. With over 20 years of experience spanning product, data, and operations, he has led high-impact go-to-market and innovation strategies for startups and global enterprises. See All Blogs

title: Colony Bank Launches Private Banking and Welcomes Colby Cardin as Private Banker
summary: Phillip Anderson joins Colony Bank as Savannah Market President, leading its banking team in Savannah, Georgia.
body_text: Colony Bank is expanding its financial services with the introduction of Private Banking, a new offering designed to provide personalized banking and financial solutions for individuals and families with more complex financial needs. As part of this expansion, the bank has welcomed Colby Cardin as Private Banker. “Private Banking is another way we’re expanding the personalized service our customers have come to expect from Colony Bank,” said D Copeland, President of Colony Bank. “As our customers’ financial needs continue to evolve, they want a trusted partner who understands their goals and can connect them with the right financial solutions. We’re excited to welcome Colby to the team and look forward to growing this offering as we continue helping our customers achieve their financial goals.” Private Banking offers personalized banking and lending solutions tailored to each client’s financial goals while connecting them with Colony Bank’s broader capabilities, including wealth management, insurance, specialized lending and more. Cardin brings 24 years of experience in the financial services industry with a unique background in both relationship banking and leadership development. His career has included roles in commercial banking, business banking, credit and underwriting, as well as executive coaching and talent development. He earned a bachelor’s degree from the University of Georgia and is a graduate of the Stonier Graduate School of Banking at the University of Pennsylvania. Cardin is also an Associate Certified Coach (ACC) Coach through the International Coaching Federation. A third generation banker and a lifelong resident of Columbus, Cardin has built his career serving the community he calls home. He currently serves on the board of Valley Healthcare System Inc. and on the faculty for the Georgia Bankers Association GBA Banking School. He previously served on the executive board of Scouts America. Cardin and his wife, Laura, who serves as the Chief Executive Officer of Pastoral Institute, have been married for 26 years and have two children. “I’ve had the opportunity to work alongside Colby, and I’ve seen firsthand the way he builds lasting relationships and earns the trust of his clients,” said Mitch Watkins, Regional President. “He’s established a strong reputation throughout the Columbus community, and we’re excited to welcome him to Colony Bank as we introduce private banking to our customers.” The addition of private banking reflects Colony Bank’s continued investment in meeting customers’ evolving financial needs. By expanding its suite of financial solutions, the bank is making it easier for customers to access personalized guidance and specialized expertise while continuing to work with a trusted local financial partner. Segment Adjusted EBITDA is the profitability metric reported to the Company's Chief Operating Decision Maker (the Company's President and Chief Executive Officer) for purposes of allocating resources and assessing segment performance. As such, it is the measure of segment profit for the Company under U.S. generally accepted accounting principles ("GAAP"). Segment Adjusted EBITDA is calculated as revenue less direct operating expenses and selling, general and administrative expenses, excluding restructuring and other costs. Restructuring and other costs include costs associated with cost-saving initiatives such as severance, consulting and termination costs, and other special costs. Non-GAAP Financial Information This earnings release includes information that does not conform to GAAP, including Adjusted EBITDA, Adjusted Corporate expenses, Funds From Operations ("FFO") and Adjusted Funds From Operations ("AFFO"). The Company believes these non-GAAP measures provide investors with useful insights into its operating performance, particularly when comparing the Company to other out-of-home advertisers, as these measures are widely used within the industry. Please refer to the reconciliations of non-GAAP financial measures to the most directly comparable GAAP measures below. The Company defines and uses these non-GAAP measures as follows: Adjusted EBITDA is defined as income (loss) from continuing operations, plus: income tax expense (benefit) attributable to continuing operations; non-operating expenses (income), including interest expense, net, and other expense (income), net; other operating expense (income), net; depreciation, amortization and impairment charges; share-based compensation expense; and restructuring and other costs, which include costs associated with cost-saving initiatives such as severance, consulting and termination costs, and other special costs. The Company uses Adjusted EBITDA to plan and forecast for future periods and as a key performance measure for executive compensation. The Company believes Adjusted EBITDA allows investors to assess the Company's performance in a way that is consistent with management's approach and facilitates comparisons to other companies with different capital structures or tax rates. Additionally, the Company believes Adjusted EBITDA is commonly used by investors, analysts and peers in the industry for valuation and performance comparisons. Adjusted Corporate expenses is defined as corporate expenses excluding share-based compensation and restructuring and other costs. The Company uses Adjusted Corporate expenses to evaluate core corporate spending and for planning and forecasting purposes. FFO is defined in accordance with the National Association of Real Estate Investment Trusts ("Nareit") as consolidated net income (loss) before: depreciation, amortization and impairment of real estate; gains or losses from the disposition of real estate; and adjustments to eliminate unconsolidated affiliates and noncontrolling interests. AFFO is defined as FFO excluding discontinued operations and before adjustments for continuing operations, including: maintenance capital expenditures; straight-line rent effects; depreciation, amortization and impairment of non-real estate; amortization of deferred financing costs and note discounts; share-based compensation; deferred income taxes; restructuring and other costs; transaction costs; and other items, such as adjustments for unconsolidated affiliates and noncontrolling interests and gains or losses from the disposition of non-real estate. Although the Company is not a Real Estate Investment Trust ("REIT"), it competes directly with REITs that present the non-GAAP measures of FFO and AFFO. Therefore, the Company believes that presenting these measures helps investors evaluate its performance on the same terms as its direct competitors. The Company calculates FFO in accordance with Nareit's definition, which does not restrict its use to REITs. Additionally, the Company believes FFO and AFFO are already commonly used by investors, analysts and competitors in the industry for valuation and performance comparisons. The Company does not use, and you should not use, FFO and AFFO as indicators of the Company's ability to fund its cash needs, pay dividends or make other distributions. Since the Company is not a REIT, it has no obligation to pay dividends and does not intend to do so in the foreseeable future. Moreover, the presentation of these measures should not be construed as an indication that the Company is currently in a position to convert into a REIT. These non-GAAP financial measures should not be considered in isolation or as substitutes for the most directly comparable GAAP measures as an indicator of operating performance or the Company's ability to fund its cash needs. In addition, these measures may not be comparable to similarly named measures presented by other companies.
